result.markdown: --- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [export_metadata()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-function} | Pointblank description: Export metadata as a Frictionless Table Schema. twitter-card: title: >- [export_metadata()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-function} | Pointblank description: Export metadata as a Frictionless Table Schema. title: >- [export_metadata()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-function} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: Export metadata as a Frictionless Table Schema. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Export metadata as a Frictionless Table Schema. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/posit-dev/pointblank/blob/main/pointblank/metadata/_export.py#L32-L155){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature export_metadata( source, destination=None, format="frictionless", **kwargs, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} The `export_metadata()` function is the reverse of [`import_metadata()`](`pointblank.import_metadata`): it writes a [`MetadataImport`](`pointblank.MetadataImport`) out in a standard format. The only format currently supported is the [Frictionless Table Schema](https://specs.frictionlessdata.io/table-schema/), a JSON description of a table's fields that many data tools can read. Because the metadata can come from any of the formats that `import_metadata()` reads, this is also a way to convert between them, for example to get a Table Schema from a CSVW file or from the variable definitions in a Define-XML document. Each variable becomes a field, with its dtype mapped to a Frictionless type (`"integer"`, `"number"`, `"string"`, `"date"` and so on) and its label and description used as the field's `title` and `description`. The constraints `required`, `unique`, `minimum`, `maximum`, `minLength`, `maxLength`, `pattern` and `enum` are written for the variables that have them, and declared missing values become the field's `missingValues`. Variables that are both required and unique make up the schema's `primaryKey`, and the dataset label and description become the schema's `title` and `description`. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [source]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [MetadataImport]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The metadata to export. To export one dataset from a [`MetadataPackage`](`pointblank.MetadataPackage`), select it first (as in `package["DM"]`). [destination]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | Path | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : A file path to write the schema to, as indented JSON. Any missing parent directories are created. If `None` (the default), nothing is written. The schema is returned in both cases. [format]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [["frictionless"]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default} : The output format. Only `"frictionless"` is supported (`"table_schema"` is accepted as another name for it). [**kwargs]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Any]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Options for the exporter. `include_constraints=False` leaves out the `constraints` of every field, giving a schema with only the field names, types, titles and missing values. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [dict]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The Table Schema as a dictionary. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the format isn't supported. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Let's import the bundled CSVW metadata for a table of weather observations and export it as a Frictionless Table Schema: ::: {#d6d30391 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import json import pointblank as pb meta = pb.import_metadata(pb.load_metadata_example("weather_csvw.json")) schema = pb.export_metadata(meta) print(json.dumps(schema["fields"][:3], indent=2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [ { "name": "station_id", "type": "string", "title": "Station ID", "constraints": { "required": true, "unique": true } }, { "name": "timestamp", "type": "datetime", "title": "Observation Time", "constraints": { "required": true, "unique": true } }, { "name": "temperature_c", "type": "number", "title": "Temperature (Celsius)", "constraints": { "required": true, "minimum": -50.0, "maximum": 60.0 } } ] ``` ::: ::: The first three fields show how the CSVW column definitions were carried over: the titles, the types (a CSVW `decimal` is a Frictionless `number`), and the constraints. The remaining keys of the schema describe the table as a whole: ::: {#caa61558 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(schema["primaryKey"]) print(schema["title"]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ['station_id', 'timestamp'] Weather Station Observations ``` ::: ::: The two required and unique columns form the primary key, and the title comes from the dataset label in the CSVW file. Give a `destination=` to write the schema to a file. Here it's written to a temporary directory and then imported again: ::: {#be893e76 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} import tempfile from pathlib import Path with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp: path = Path(tmp) / "weather_schema.json" pb.export_metadata(meta, destination=path, include_constraints=False) reimported = pb.import_metadata(path) print(reimported.variable_names) print(reimported.get_variable("temperature_c").min_val) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ['station_id', 'timestamp', 'temperature_c', 'humidity_pct', 'wind_speed_kmh', 'precipitation_mm', 'condition'] None ``` ::: ::: The file is a standalone Table Schema, so `import_metadata()` reads it back with the same variables. With `include_constraints=False` the range of `temperature_c` wasn't written, so its `min_val` is now `None`. That's useful when you want to share the structure of a table without the rules for its values. ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~import_metadata`) : Read metadata from a file. [](`~MetadataImport`) : The metadata that is exported.
